method: A dolly zoom holds the subject at the same size while the camera moves toward or away and the lens zooms the other way. The thin-lens transverse magnification of an object at distance d in front of a lens is m = f / (d - f), so holding m constant across a move from d1 to d2 gives the end focal length f2 = f1 x d2 / d1 exactly, and the zoom ratio equals the dolly ratio: 50 mm at 3 m matches 25 mm at 1.5 m, and 35 mm at 2 m matches 70 mm at 4 m. The same rule is applied at each quarter step of the move for the position table, so every row keeps the subject's framing. A background plane at distance D has its own magnification f / (D - f); the page reports its size at the end as a percentage of its size at the start, relative to the subject, so a dolly-in with zoom-out shrinks the background (the classic Vertigo effect) and a dolly-out with zoom-in enlarges it. A background far behind the subject changes by almost exactly the zoom ratio, while a close one changes a little more than that ratio. Focal lengths are 4 to 1200 mm, distances 0.2 to 1000 m and the background 0.5 to 5000 m; the background must lie beyond the subject at both ends, the start and end distances must differ, and the focal length must be shorter than the start distance so that a real image forms. Distances are measured from the lens rather than the camera body, and the subject is treated as flat at its stated distance: focus, depth of field, lens zoom curves, focus breathing, rolling shutter and the framing of the subject's own edges are not modelled. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Dolly zoom: the camera dollies toward or away from the subject while the lens zooms so that the subject stays the same size in the frame, in the dolly-in/zoom-out and dolly-out/zoom-in forms
Wikipedia, Magnification: photographic transverse magnification M = f / (d_o - f) = h_i / h_o, the relation inverted here to hold the subject's image size constant
